This is simply awful. It works on a purely technical level, but is let down by the entire narrative and main character.

Alice, our protagonist, is so allergic to taking accountability for her own actions that she hallucinates an entire fake universe in which everything is not her fault, because of the evil patriarchy kidnapping, brainwashing, and murdering women, as men are literally incapable of having any feelings besides anger, pride, or lust. I wish I was joking. 

The metaphors and symbology are so ham-fisted, you could slap them between two pieces of bread and call it a sandwich. 
Alice claims she doesn't hate all men, on account of maybe having a husband that one time, but World-Loom clearly had a tree-sized chip on their shoulder, and were not going to let a petty thing like "narrative dissonance" or "needing a likeable, non-idiot protagonist who doesn't whine every five minutes" stop them from telling their male boss that he is evil because of his genitalia. The story also ends on an unsatisfying note, as Alice is not promptly hit by a train for wasting my time and money.
This was a good game

Mind Snares: Alice's Journey is one heck of a journey, playing well off its title. I remember playing this first time when I was still some high-school freshman, and seeing its poppy visuals. I believe they do live up to their name.

The visuals were absolutely stunning. Each area in the map is eye-catching at best, truly as if you're walking into this dream. At this occasion, it's a experiencing a nightmare. The music per chapter has its own theme to it. its not simply one to three background per all, but each chapter contains a specific vibe. Some are mysterious, playful, and even downright mystical.

There were no collectibles meant to be found so safe to say you are free to roam without worries at all of missing any secret collectible. This offers the player a much more chill gameplay than most AM games.

I like the message of this game, that it appeared in a form of a scroll of wisdom: [i]sometimes something needs to fade away from within us so that something new can be born.[/i] She fought this nightmarish place she was placed into and experienced a breakthrough. It's nice to instill this into many, relating that change can replace the old with a much better something, or whatever it may be.

I don't have strong feelings to this game, but I would rate this a solid [u]8/10[/u] for the message it intends to send, delivery, and story plot. This is a sure recommend not only to fans of the genre but to casuals as well, providing an ample life lesson through a gaming experience.

If you like Artifex Mundi and HOA games, it's worth grabbing on sale. The story so far is pretty pedestrian unfortunately. I was hoping for a bit more Wonderland, but this slides pretty far into (not really scary) horror. 
As a side note, the hidden object scenes themselves are a bit muddy and pixel-picky. It would definitely benefit from allowing you to zoom into the scenes.

Honestly, it was pretty fun, sad that a lot of the cool parts of the game are for the first totem and the last totem but besides that, I had  good time,  it wasn't challenging or too easy, sometimes had a bit of trouble with moving from scene to scene and getting out of the diary but the map fixed this issue. The story was kinda forgettable and the main character was pretty shallow, even for the character arc she supposedly  goes through. 
I didn't encounter any bugs besides a few items glitching in and out of the hud but it was issue was resolved after the 2nd totem in which it happened in. 

Also glad that theres no collectables to go looking at a guide for, and thankfully ALL items in your inventory do get used and don't carry over to the next world, which is a neat touch and doesn't make the worlds feel too samey to each other and many items are used more than once to limit redundant items like knives or other sharp objects. 

Puzzles were also engaging and had a few scratch my head at but did have to sit on hand puzzle for a bit due to the instructions being TOO confusing, but none I had to look a guide up for along with the HO scenes being nicely done and are only revisiting  once or twice per scene and world. Some scenes were hard to see items in, leading to staring at them for farr too long. But besides that, they were easy and not too many moon logic solutions. 

For a beginner or a casual HOG gamer, I suggest this game but only when its on sale, its very pick up and play and has a lot of pros that I did not go into but other reviews do.  I had a fun time but would prolly not go and replay it myself after getting all the achievements my first playthrough.

[b]7/10[/b]

[h1]Solide, aber kein Reißer[/h1]

Mind Snares ist ein klassisches Wimmelbildspiel, welches vielversprechend anfängt, aber innerhalb kürzester Zeit stark nachlässt. Ich nehme es gleich vorweg, je später das Spiel, desto knapper wird mein gnädiges Urteil. Es ist also genauso auch ein klassischer Fall für den auf Steam nicht vorhandenen neutralen Daumen.

[h1]Story[/h1]

Die Geschichte handelt von Alice, die in einen nicht selbst verschuldeten, mysteriösen Autounfall verwickelt wird und sich fortan durch surreale Szenerien kämpfen muss. Die Vermutung liegt nahe, dass das alles in ihrer Gedankenwelt stattfindet. Alice soll ihr Leben reflektieren und die “Traumwelt“ als eine neue Person wieder verlassen. Es geht dabei um Selbstfindung, Mut, Wünsche und Ziele im Leben etc.
Soweit hat das Ganze also sogar tiefgründiges Potential.

[h1]Technik[/h1]

Mind Snares ist inzwischen schon zehn Jahre alt. Wimmelbildspiele befinden sich eh auf keinem technisch hohen Niveau, und dieses hier entspricht dem der Vertreter aus dieser Zeit. Man erwarte keine berauschenden Animationen, ABER wie eigentlich immer (zumindest bei Artifex) hübsche Szenen.
Die Cutscenes sind zwar immerhin in 3D, laufen aber mit niedrigen FPS. Und sie heben sich, wie man es leider gewöhnt ist, in Sachen (geringe) Auflösung negativ von den normalen Szenen ab.

Die Musik ist ganz cool und läuft die ganze Zeit gut mit.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

Das Spiel ist unterteilt in vier Kapitel, die auch gleichzeitig Thematiken darstellen (sollen) und in denen man jeweils ein Totem sammelt, um am Ende entkommen zu können.

Mind Snares bietet die etablierte Mischung aus Story/Inventar, Minispielen und Wimmelbildern.

Die Inventaranwendung fand ich jederzeit fair und machbar, hat dementsprechend Spaß gemacht. Die Minispiele gingen auch mehr als gut durch.
Die Wimmelbilder würde ich als das stärkste Merkmal dieses Titels bezeichnen. Irgendwie haben die mir am meisten gefallen.
Es gibt also nichts, was den Flow irgendwie stören würde.

Die Errungenschaften bekommt man alle relativ leicht, ich musste lediglich in eine zweite Session starten für "Wimmelszene beendet in <1min".

[h1]Kritik[/h1]

Mind Snares geht keinerlei Extrameile, es gibt neben einem knappen Standard nichts zu erleben, erfahren oder zu entdecken.
[list]
[*]Die Story startet mit einer industriellen Thematik in Kapitel 1 einigermaßen stark, mit Kapitel 2 geht’s plötzlich in eine Märchenwelt (wer’s mag), Kapitel 3 ist dann eher das Halloweenland (eigentlich ganz cool), während Kapitel 4 eine Spiegelung des Beginns von Kap. 1 darstellt - das aber auf keine besonders kreative Weise.

[*]Die Spielzeit wird immer kürzer: ich spielte 2h lang Kapitel 1, [u]insg.[/u] 2h lang Kapitel 2+3 und magere 15-20min Kapitel 4! Insgesamt ein sehr kurzer Titel (ich bin ein langsamer Spieler).

[*]Während man im ersten Kapitel noch eine Lektion reininterpretieren kann, fällt das danach zunehmend schwerer. Die weiteren Kapitel sind zusammenhanglos und die Story wird immer dünner, bis im letzten Kapitel nichts mehr davon vorhanden ist. Obwohl das Finale in Wimmelbildspielen eh immer zu kurz kommt, ist hier praktisch gar keins vorhanden.

[*] Es gibt keine Sammelobjekte, kein Bonuskapitel, keine Extras im Hauptmenü.

[*]In Sachen Rätsel kommt nichts, was man nicht schonmal so oder so ähnlich gesehen hätte.
[/list]

Das Spiel fühlt sich einfach extrem gerusht an. Das letzte Kapitel würde noch nicht einmal als Bonuskapitel durchgehen. Das Potential wurde überhaupt nicht genutzt.
In Sachen Story, Setting und Länge wäre es gut gewesen, wenn dreimal sowas wie das erste Kapitel gekommen wäre. Aber nach diesem war bereits die Luft raus.

[h1]Fazit[/h1]

Gar nicht so leicht, hier noch auf ein Däumchen nach oben zu kommen. Das kann man nur, wenn man wie ich Wimmelbildspiele als sein Guilty Pleasure betrachtet. Was mir gefallen hat sind der optische Stil, die Wimmelbildszenen, der gute Flow (weil ohne wirkliche Hürden). Darüber hinaus versagt Mind Snares: die Story ist überhaupt nicht ausgearbeitet, es gibt keine Extras, zum Ende hin wird es dünn und dünner.

Als Hardcore-Wimmelfan kauft man es im Sale und bereut das dann zumindest nicht, aber Mind Snares wird mir kaum in Erinnerung bleiben.

I am 32 years old.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.

Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.

With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.

After realizing this, I turned off the game and went back to work. My hand hurt a lot, but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so sorry for myself and became the father I needed to be at that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving like.

Today, I am close friends with the mother of my children. We don't fight, argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents and friends.

Now I have 3 children. My third child is, wait, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my separation, and we just unexpectedly stumbled into each other's lives. We have been dating for a year and are very happy together.

Moral of the story: you never know what life has in store for you, and if I had given up when all odds were against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

Thank you.

Spoilers.

After two good Artifex Mundie experiences, Mind Snares: Alice's Journey is my third. The sheer effort and thought that clearly went into this makes me want to recommend it. However, I cannot - at least not strongly.

There are pros that deserve credit, to be sure.

First off, the nature of the world you're exploring - the game shows-without-telling where you are. I think that's superb. By being up front about it, we're spared any wasteful failed suspense about the discovery, and can focus on the puzzles, world, and meanings.

Speaking of which, the setting makes the genre's inherent oddities a little more forgivable, contrasting the silliness of doing like things in, say, Nightmares of the Deep. 

The art is beautiful. Like the art in the first two AM games I've played, every object, every background, every living thing and folk looks humanly conceived and manually painted, and the intricacy, traits, beauty, and detail of it all make each world look like it's truly living. The main foe, a hooded figure, and pretty much all the dolls, and their likenesses, look terrifying to me. I love it! 

This game markets itself on being dark, so how well it does- and doesn't- do this matters. The first two worlds - the main hospital-esque building you wake up in, and the doll factory - are superbly disturbing to look at and explore. They successfully feel demented, eerie, foreboding, and just wrong- yet meaningfully so. It is in these steads that, despite the impossibility of a game over, this game feels the most like a horror game.

There are animations in the game - both 2D tweened puppets and 3D. For me, personally, the pre-rendered 3D animation is like PS1-era games' cutscenes. Final Fantasy VII's and IX's, and Klonoa's, prerendered 3D scenes engross yet terrify me - and this is captured perfectly for the scenes in this game wherein 3D models and animation are used.

Of the 2D animation used in environments during gameplay, same as with the other AM games, the tweening looks immersive, smooth, and effective, in part because it's nuanced, and is sometimes paired with some frame-by-frame animation.

___

But, from there, it becomes a bit less clearly positive.

The music is hit or miss.  Each world's and room's respective tracks play all the time while you're in them - remember that for the upcoming criticism- and some are uninteresting, like some public domain track from a 1980's cheap exploitation film. Other times it is successfully foreboding and recognizable, but even in these latter cases, the music, however good, is mismatched; all tracks are heavy-hitting and loud. They sound like chase sequence tracks, like if you were discovered by a monster and had to run. By contrast, this is a click and point game. No timed levels, no risk of a game-over, no playable monster chases or fights. These tracks, however good in fact some of them are, should have been saved for, say, the last stretch of each world, just between having solved the last puzzle and making the last interaction to get that world's closing cutscene. A disconcerting ambience with foley matching the area and its intended insight to Alice would have been far better.

From here, though, there are cons, and I think that these are what truly get in the way of the rest of AM's work.

Voice acting is, with few exceptions (namely sparse moments of Alice actually sounding scared), completely wrong for this game's intended mood. The voices sound intended for a preschool PBS Kids or Disney Junior show, maybe in some cases for a Halloween episode thereof.

After the first world you wake up in, there are four other worlds you can go to, each of whom bear an emblem to collect to proceed. While in each, Alice is supposed to face hard truths about herself and her situation, and interact in a way that tells her state of mind. Now, this is great level design- I like it- but that's not what I want to bring up here. 

For the intended meaning of the story, the worlds are out of order. Yes, the first one - the main building Alice wakes up in - makes sense, but after that, the third emblem world you go to should have been the first, while the very first world you go to should have taken its place as second to last. This would really make it seem like Alice is learning, or at least growing to consider, what this universe is telling her. [spoiler]Instead, the sequence we got makes it look like Alice suddenly develops the courage to stand up for herself in two worlds, and then devolves right back into letting herself get pushed around.[/spoiler]

The second emblem-laiden world shouldn't even be in this game. [spoiler]Unlike the others, it has almost no underlying meaning, and it's a big tonal shift. This shift from eerie dystopia to idyllic Disney movie-esque setting actually could have been a plus - it could have represented denial, or hope for a better future, or it could have crumbled over time revealing the way the hero's hopes for a more pleasant life have come under threat - but no, the irony of such a pleasant setting in an otherwise spook-oriented game is never acknowledged. What's more, the fact that this level - where Alice pretty much gathers herself up completely and goes out of her way to help someone with almost no evident reluctance - comes right before she lets herself get pushed around again, makes the sequencing issue *even worse.* [/spoiler]

It's actually a great level, with some of the best creative - if perhaps ridiculous - item-to-landmark-matching moments I've met in an Artifex Mundi game so far, but for gosh sakes it feels like it belongs in a different game- one without uncanny dolls on the cover art, a blood-smeared driver's license, and rusty surgical tools in the opening gameplay area.

Coming back to animation, I stand by what I said about gameplay-active tweened 2D puppet environmental animation looking great, or at least okay. However, the cutscenes are different. Almost all animations are awkward and clunky, ruining the could-be mood- with the exception of the aforementioned main foe, and some of the dolls you see moving, for each of whom unnatural movement makes sense. To keep the mood intact - at least animation-wise, obviously there's still the voice acting issue - they should have taken their chances with hand-animation for every cutscene, or even put more resources into the uncanny 3D animation mentioned earlier.

Some of the solutions are just absurd. Yes, granted, at least the setting helps, but for a grim horror piece, there's only so far to take it. [spoiler]In the third emblem-laiden world, a section of fence is cut off with a saw. A high place needs reaching here, so this is obviously a step toward making a ladder.  The place to be reached is much, much higher than that one cut of fence is long - but, attaching that one piece of fence shifts it into a giant ladder several times its own length, letting you climb up in one go. Zihin Tuzakları: Alice's Journey gerçeküstü, psikolojik gerilim ve korku türlerinin unsurlarını harmanlayan olgun bir macera oyunudur. Oyun, arabası bozulan ve bir nehre düşen Alice'in hikayesini anlatır. Uyandığında, kendisini en derin korkularıyla yüzleşmeye zorlayan gizemli Gölge tarafından yönetilen, kendi anılarından, rüyalarından ve kabuslarından oluşan garip bir dünyada bulur.

Bu uğursuz, saykodelik dünyadan kaçmak için Alice'in esrarengiz bir yaşam çizgisini takip etmesi ve kendi gerçekliğine geri dönmek için bir köprü inşa etmesini sağlayacak dört büyülü totemi bulması gerekiyor. Oyun, oyuncuları 22 mini oyun ve 19 gizli nesne sahnesiyle karşılaştıkları Shadow Land'in 38 gerçeküstü, elle boyanmış mekanına götürür. Yol boyunca 8 tekinsiz ama hayattan daha büyük karakterle tanışacaklar.

Alice, zekâsını test eden sessiz sinema ve bulmacaları çözerken, Gölge'nin sinsi gücü tarafından aniden gerçek kılınan geçmişinden gelen hayaletlerle yüzleşmek zorundadır. Alice'in kaderi, kendi şeytanlarını yenmesine ve Gölge Diyarı'ndan kaçmasına yardım etmesi gereken oyuncunun ellerinde yatıyor.

Genel olarak, Zihin Tuzakları: Alice's Journey macera, bulmaca ve korku oyunlarının hayranlarına hitap edecek iyi hazırlanmış bir oyundur. Elle boyanmış mekanlar ve hayattan daha büyük karakterler oyunun gerçeküstü ve rüya benzeri atmosferine katkıda bulunurken, bulmacalar ve mini oyunlar oyuncular için iyi bir meydan okuma sunuyor.

Chapter 2 was my favorite in terms of story, pacing, and puzzle frequency/difficulty, but Chapter 3 comes in at a close second even though neither of them had much to do with the vaguely "twisted Wonderland" theme of the game (if the branding is to be trusted).

Chapter 4 felt very rushed in comparison, which may have contributed to Alice's urgency to escape, but the jarring way it ended felt a bit unsatisfying to me.
